quote: The Day of Atonement is needed by all who have sinned, and therefore among the solemnities of the law, which contain the figures of the heavenly mysteries, there is held a certain solemnity which is called the Day of Atonement. This, then, which has now been read out, is the legislation of that very solemnity which, as we have said, is called the Day of Atonement. But let us see first what the content of the letter itself intends, so that, while you pray — provided that you so beseech the Lord that you may deserve to be heard — we may be able to receive the grace of the Spirit, through which we may have strength to explain the mysteries which are contained in the law. "Two sons of Aaron died, Nadab and Abihu, when they offered strange fire at the altar of the Lord." It was necessary that Aaron should be instructed by heavenly teaching in what manner he ought to approach the altar, and…

But first of all let us show how these things which are written concerning the sacrifices the Apostle says are "figures" and "forms", whose truth is shown in other things, lest perchance the hearers should think that we presume and violently bend the law of God to another sense than that in which it is written — that is, if no Apostolic authority in these things which we assert should go before. Paul therefore, writing to the Hebrews, namely to those who indeed read the law and had these things meditated upon and well known, but had need of understanding as to how one ought to think concerning the sacrifices, says in this manner: "for Jesus entered not into the holy place made with hands, the copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us." And again he says of the victims: "for this he did once, by offering himself as a…

Now indeed concerning the victims, some are commanded to be the high priest's own, but others are "to be taken from the people". His own is said to be the "bull-calf", which among animals is more precious and stronger; and the second animal, the "ram", which among sheep is without doubt more precious. But from the people the gifts are commanded to be offered: a "ram" from the leaders and "two goats" from the people; one that is to be sent away "into the wilderness", which is also named "the scapegoat", and one that is to be offered to the Lord. If the whole people of God were holy and all were blessed, there would not be made two lots over the goats, and one indeed bear the lot to be sent away "into the wilderness", but the other to be offered "to the Lord", but there would be one lot and one victim to the Lord alone. But now, since in the multitude of those who approach the Lord there…

But that which we say concerning the lot, let not the hearer take it as though some such lot is meant as is wont to be conducted among men by chance and not by judgment. "The Lord's lot" is to be taken as though one should say the choice of the Lord or the portion of the Lord, and again the lot of that one which is sent "into the wilderness" is to be taken as that portion which, for its own unworthiness, is spurned and cast off by the Lord. For indeed the very word "scapegoat" contains the signification of one cast off and rejected. From which we can also understand this, for example: an evil thought ascends into your heart, a desire of another man's wife or of a neighbor's possession; understand at once that this is of "the lot of the scapegoat", cast it off immediately and expel it from your heart. How do you cast it off? If you have with you the hand of the "ready man", that is, if…

Yet since the word of God is rich and, according to the judgment of Solomon, is to be "inscribed upon the heart" not simply, but doubly and "triply," let us try even now to add some things to those which were spoken a while ago according to our strength, that we may show how, "in a type of things to come," here too one goat was offered to the Lord as a victim and the other was sent away "alive." Hear in the Gospels Pilate saying to the priests and the people of the Jews: "Which of the two do you wish that I release to you, Jesus who is called Christ, or Barabbas?" Then all the people cried out that he should release "Barabbas," but hand Jesus over to death. Behold, you have the goat which was sent away "alive into the wilderness," bearing with itself the sins of the people that cried out and said: "Crucify, crucify!" This, then, is the goat sent away "alive into the wilderness," and the…

May I offer, moreover, an interpretation of the two goats which were presented on "the great day of atonement"? Do they not also prefigure the two natures of Christ? They were of like size and very similar in appearance, owing to the Lord's identity of aspect. He is not to come in any other form. He had to be recognized by those by whom he was also wounded and pierced. One of these goats was bound with scarlet and driven by the people out of the camp into the wilderness, amid cursing, and spitting, and pulling and piercing, being thus marked with all the signs of the Lord's own passion. The other, by being offered up for sins and given to the priests of the temple for meat, afforded proofs of his second appearance, when (after all sins have been expiated) the priests of the spiritual temple, that is, the church, are to enjoy the flesh, as it were, of the Lord's own grace. The rest will…

I will however mention the sacrifice in which two goats were offered, the one being slain and the other let go. In these two goats there is an anticipative image of the two natures of the Savior; in the one let go, of the impassible Godhead, in the one slain, of the passible manhood.

Let us see after these things what the things are which the high priest does: "and he shall take" it says "a censer full of coals of fire from the altar which is before the Lord". We read also in Isaiah that the prophet is purged by fire through "one of the seraphim, which was sent to him, when it took with tongs one coal from those which were upon the altar, and touched the lips of the prophet and said": "behold, I have taken away your iniquities". To me these things seem to be mystical and to indicate this, that to each one, according to that in which he sins, if he is worthy to be purified, coals are applied to his members. For since the prophet here says: "I have unclean lips, and I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", therefore the "coal taken up with the tongs" by the seraph purges his lips, in which alone he professes himself not to be clean. From which it is…

"And he shall take" it says "a censer full of coals". Not all are purged by that fire which is taken "from the altar". Aaron is purged by that fire, and Isaiah, and any who are like them; but others, who are not such, among whom I reckon even myself, we shall be purged by another fire — I fear lest by that of which it is written: "a river of fire ran before him". That "fire" is not "from the altar". The fire which is "from the altar" is the fire of the Lord; but that which is outside the altar is not the Lord's, but is the proper fire of each one of those who sin, of which it is said: "their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished". That "fire" therefore is of those very ones who kindled it, as also elsewhere it is written: "walk in your fire and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves". But to Isaiah not his own fire is applied, but the fire of the…

Therefore the high priest "takes a censer full of coals of fire from the altar which is before the Lord, and fills his hand with the fine incense of composition and carries it into the interior of the veil". Let us understand first what the history designates, and then let us inquire what the spiritual sense holds. Twofold is the house of the tabernacle of testimony or of the temple of the Lord. The first is that in which is the "altar of the whole burnt offerings", which is stirred up with perpetual fires, in which house it is lawful for the priests alone to stand and to celebrate the rites and ministries of the sacrifices, and to neither the Levites nor anyone else besides is access granted. But the second house is the interior one, separated from this only by a "veil". Within which veil are the "ark of the testament" and the "propitiatory", upon which the "two cherubim" are set, and…

The divine word therefore says: "and he shall place incense upon the fire in the sight of the Lord, and the smoke of the incense shall cover the propitiatory which is over the testimonies, and he shall not die. And he shall take of the blood of the bull-calf and shall sprinkle with his finger upon the propitiatory toward the east". The rite indeed of atonement for men among the ancients, which was made to God, he has taught how it should be celebrated; but you, who have come to Christ, the true high priest, who by his blood made God propitious to you and reconciled you to the Father, do not cling to the blood of the flesh; but learn rather the blood of the Word, and hear him saying to you: "this is my blood, which shall be poured out for you for the remission of sins". He who is imbued with the mysteries knows both the flesh and the blood of the Word of God. Let us not therefore linger…

After these things the Scripture adds: "and there shall not be" it says "a man, when the high priest enters within the interior veil in the tabernacle of testimony". How "shall there not be a man"? I understand it thus, that he who has been able to follow Christ and to penetrate with him the interior tabernacle and to ascend the heights of the heavens, shall now "not be a man", but according to his own word shall be "as an angel of God". Or perhaps even that word will be fulfilled concerning him which the Lord himself said: "I said, you are gods and sons of the Most High, all of you". Whether therefore, made spiritual, he becomes one spirit with the Lord, or through the glory of the resurrection passes into the order of angels, rightly he will now "not be a man"; but each one himself provides this for himself, that he either exceed the appellation of man or be reckoned within the…

But let us see who this is who receives that one whose "lot has become the scapegoat's", that he may cast him "into the wilderness". "A man" it says "ready shall receive the goat which has come into his lot, upon whom the lot of the scapegoat has fallen, and shall lead him away into the wilderness." The end of this lot is the "wilderness", that is, a deserted place, deserted of virtues, deserted of God, deserted of righteousness, deserted of Christ, deserted of every good. And so upon each of us too awaits one lot of the two. For either, acting well, we are "the Lord's lot", or, acting badly, our lot leads us "to the wilderness". Do you wish that I show you evidently how those two lots are always at work and each one of us becomes either "the Lord's lot" or "the scapegoat's" or "the wilderness'"? Consider in the Gospels that "rich man" living "splendidly" and luxuriously, and "Lazarus…

Perhaps in another way also "the man ready" and clean, who "leads away that one whose lot has come, into the wilderness", and by that very act by which he leads him out, as one who has touched something unclean, is said to "wash his garments" at evening and to be clean — perhaps even our Lord and Savior himself may be understood, in that part in which he took on the "garments" of our nature, that is, of flesh and blood, which he "washed at evening"; on account of which also the prophet had long ago said of him: "and I saw Jesus the great priest, clothed in filthy garments, and the devil standing at his right hand, that he might contradict him." Therefore he "washed his robe in wine" — that is, in his own blood — "at evening", and was made "clean". And thence perhaps it was that after the resurrection he said to Mary, who wished to hold his feet: "do not touch me." But do you wish to see…

"On the days of your solemn feasts you shall mortify yourselves." Why did he say this? Because fasts and vigils and holy mortifications afflict bodies that are humbled, but they purify hearts that have been defiled. They may take strength away from limbs, but they add a bright sheen to conscience. Sins of pleasure are redeemed by bodily weariness while the physical delights of dissipation are punished by the distresses of a hard cross. Thus by present mortification the sentence of future death is suspended.

We indeed, who are of the Church, rightly receive Moses and read his writings, understanding this about him: that he is a prophet, and that, by God's revealing to him, he wrote down in symbols and figures and allegorical forms the mysteries to come, which we teach to have been fulfilled in their own time. But whoever does not receive in him a meaning of this kind, whether he be one of the Jews or even one of our own, cannot show him to be a prophet at all; for how will he prove him a prophet, whose letters he asserts to be commonplace, aware of nothing future and containing no hidden mystery? And so, as this man who thinks in this way reads these things, the divine word rebukes him and says: "Do you suppose you understand what you read?" There is, then, the law, and all the things that are in the law, according to the Apostle's judgment, "imposed until the time of correction"; and just…

Ours, therefore — that is, we who do not "serve the shadow and the copy," but the truth — this is the Day of Atonement for us, on which the remission of sins has been given to us, when "Christ our Passover has been sacrificed." How then, having come to know the truth, "do we turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements of this world, to which you wish to be enslaved anew from the beginning, observing days and months and seasons and years?" Hear how the prophet too rejects a fast of this kind and says: "This is not the fast I have chosen, says the Lord, nor a day for a man to humble his soul." You, if you wish to fast according to Christ and "to humble your soul," every time of the whole year lies open to you; nay rather, have all the days of your whole life "for humbling your soul," if indeed you "have learned" from the Lord our Savior "that he is meek and humble of heart." When,…
